chapters.title: Real Numbers
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what the chapter is about; prime factorisation and the fundamental theorem; using prime factorisation for hcf and lcm; irrational numbers and a useful theorem.

lessons.title: What the chapter is about

activities.prompt: How can we uncover the hidden building blocks of numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The big ideas
activities.body: Class IX maths began exploring irrational numbers and real numbers. This chapter starts with two properties of positive integers. Euclid’s division algorithm divides integers, leaving a smaller remainder. It helps find the HCF, the highest shared factor of two positive integers. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic connects multiplication with unique prime-factor products. These ideas prove some familiar numbers irrational. They show how a denominator’s prime factorisation affects its decimal expansion.
keyPoints: Euclid’s division algorithm concerns divisibility and has many applications.
The HCF is the highest shared factor of two positive integers.
Unique prime-factor products help prove irrationality and reveal decimal expansion.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect divisibility, prime factors and decimal expansions.

lessons.title: Prime factorisation and the Fundamental Theorem

activities.prompt: Why does every number have one special set of building blocks?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Breaking numbers into prime factors
activities.body: Factorisation means breaking a positive integer into factors. Any natural number can be written as a product of prime factors. Prime factors may repeat as often as needed. Together, these ideas show that every composite number can be factorised using primes. The prime factorisation is unique, except for the order of its factors. Combining primes in different ways can produce infinitely many numbers.
keyPoints: Factorising means breaking a positive integer into factors.
Prime factors may repeat as needed.
Each prime factorisation is unique apart from order.
activities.explanation: These ideas are the heart of prime factorisation.

lessons.title: Using prime factorisation for HCF and LCM

activities.prompt: Can prime factors help us find the HCF and LCM of two numbers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Prime factorisation and common multiples
activities.body: Prime factorisation splits a composite number into prime factors. Combining equal prime factors gives powers of primes. Once the factors are in ascending order, meaning smallest to largest, the factorisation is unique. It cannot take another form. The prime factorisation method can find both HCF and LCM. For 6 and 20, the HCF is 2.
keyPoints: Prime factorisation splits a composite number into prime factors.
Equal prime factors can be combined into powers of primes.
The prime factorisation method can find both HCF and LCM.
The HCF of 6 and 20 is 2.
activities.explanation: Wonderful start! These ideas connect prime factors with HCF and LCM.

activities.prompt: A shop has 4 red beads and 6 blue beads, and makes the greatest possible number of equal-sized sets for each colour, using every bead. How many sets does it make?
steps: The bead counts are 4 and 6, with 4 = 2 x 2 and 6 = 3 x 2.
Prime factorise both counts and take each common prime with its greater power; this gives the common part 2.
Therefore, the greatest number of sets is 2.

activities.title: Finding the LCM from the HCF
activities.body: The prime factorisation method can find both HCF and LCM for two positive integers. For 6 and 20, the HCF is 2. Their product is 120. Since HCF multiplied by LCM equals the product, divide 120 by 2. This gives an LCM of 60. You can also find the LCM directly from the HCF and the two integers.
keyPoints: The product of 6 and 20 is 120.
HCF multiplied by LCM equals the product.
Dividing 120 by 2 gives an LCM of 60.
The LCM can be found from the HCF and the integers.
activities.explanation: You have spotted a useful relationship! It connects the HCF, LCM, and product.

activities.title: Irrational numbers and prime factors
activities.body: An irrational number cannot be written as p divided by q. Here, p and q are integers, and q is not zero. Also, √p is irrational whenever p is prime. The theorem says if a prime p divides a squared, then p divides a. Its proof starts with the prime factorisation of a, meaning a product of primes. This creates a contradiction, so √2 is not rational. Therefore, √2 is irrational.

lessons.title: Irrational expressions, summary and three-number results

activities.prompt: Could an irrational number hide inside a simple-looking expression?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Irrational expressions and proofs
activities.body: An irrational number stays irrational when multiplied or divided by a non-zero rational number. The difference between 5 and √3 is irrational. A proof begins by assuming this difference is rational. It then uses coprime integers a and b. For three positive integers, HCF times LCM does not always hold. The three-number LCM uses p, q, r and their HCF. The three-number HCF uses their pairwise LCMs.
keyPoints: A non-zero rational number and an irrational number give an irrational result.
The difference between 5 and √3 is irrational.
The three-number HCF and LCM formulas need special care.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas you will use in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A ribbon is 5 cm long. Another is √3 cm long. Is their difference irrational?
steps: Suppose the difference 5 − √3 is rational.
Write it as a/b, where a and b are coprime integers.
Then √3 = 5 − a/b is rational because the fraction is rational.
But √3 is irrational, so the difference 5 − √3 is irrational.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Three-number results and the summary
activities.body: For three positive integers, HCF times LCM does not always hold. The three-number LCM formula includes p, q, r and their HCF. The three-number HCF formula uses the product of three pairwise LCMs. The summary repeats that every composite number has a unique prime factorisation.
keyPoints: The HCF-LCM rule does not always hold for three positive integers.
Three-number formulas use products, HCF and pairwise LCMs.
Every composite number has a unique prime factorisation.
activities.explanation: This card links the summary with the three-number formulas.

activities.prompt: What is the product of a non-zero rational number and an irrational number?

An irrational number

activities.context: A packaging worker has two counts of identical items and wants to arrange them into equal groups. Checking one count against the other with Euclid’s division algorithm shows whether the division is exact; any remainder must be smaller than the divisor. The worker also needs the highest common factor of the counts. In another task, a familiar irrational number is written as a fraction, and the worker examines the denominator’s prime factors before deciding how to justify its irrationality.
activities.prompt: If dividing one count by the other leaves a non-zero remainder, what should the worker conclude?
options: The two counts do not divide evenly under that division.

why.The remainder is large enough to form an: The remainder is smaller than the divisor, so it cannot form another complete divisor-sized group.
why.The remainder can be treated as another: A remainder is a leftover amount, not an additional divisor.
why.The divisor should be replaced by the re: Replacing the divisor would change the division being checked.

activities.explanation: A non-zero remainder means that the division is not exact.

activities.context: A packaging worker has two counts of identical items and wants to arrange them into equal groups. Checking one count against the other with Euclid’s division algorithm shows whether the division is exact; any remainder must be smaller than the divisor. The worker also needs the highest common factor of the counts. In another task, a familiar irrational number is written as a fraction, and the worker examines the denominator’s prime factors before deciding how to justify its irrationality.

options: Use its prime factors and the theorem to support the irrationality proof.
Declare the denominator itself irrational without further proof.

why.Declare the denominator itself irrationa: The irrationality of the denominator does not automatically prove that the number is irrational.
why.Assume that every denominator must be pr: The theorem states that composite numbers have unique prime-factor products; it does not require every denominator to be prime.
why.Use Euclid’s division algorithm to find: The algorithm concerns divisibility, while finding the decimal expansion is associated with the denominator’s prime factorisation.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Euclid’s division algorithm and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
activities.answer: Euclid’s division algorithm concerns the divisibility of integers. When a positive integer is divided by another positive integer, the remainder is smaller than the divisor. It has many applications involving divisibility, including finding the HCF of two positive integers. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic is connected with multiplication. It states that every composite number has a unique product of prime factors. The theorem also helps prove that many familiar numbers are irrational, and a denominator’s prime factorisation reveals the nature of its decimal expansion.
points: The division algorithm concerns divisibility and remainders smaller than the divisor.
Finding the HCF is an important application of the algorithm.
The theorem concerns multiplication and the unique product of prime factors of a composite number.
The theorem supports irrationality proofs and links denominator factorisation to decimal expansions.

activities.context: At a school number fair, a student is preparing display cards for 32760. The activity guide gives the prime powers in 32760 as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 13, so the student plans to draw a factor tree. A neighbouring display uses 123456789, which can be written as a product of three prime numbers. The student must explain that prime factors may repeat and that changing their order does not change the prime factorisation.
activities.prompt: If the prime factors in a completed factor tree are rearranged, what will happen?
options: The prime factorisation remains the same apart from order.
Repeated prime factors can be left out without changing the product.
The number of prime factors changes when they are rearranged.
Each new order is counted as a different prime factorisation.

why.Repeated prime factors can be left out w: Removing a repeated factor would change the product.
why.The number of prime factors changes when: Rearranging does not change how many factors there are.
why.Each new order is counted as a different: Different orders are not different prime factorisations.

activities.explanation: Uniqueness means that order alone does not create a new factorisation.

activities.context: At a school number fair, a student is preparing display cards for 32760. why.The arrangement becomes a new prime fact: New arrangements are not new prime factorisations.
why.The product must be split again to resto: The product already shows its three prime-number factors, so another split is unnecessary.
why.Only the first prime factor should appea: All three prime-number factors should be included in the product.

activities.explanation: Only the order can change because the factorisation is unique apart from order.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes.
Reason (R): Every positive integer can be written as a product of its prime factors.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the general prime-factor fact explains the composite-number statement.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Different orders of the prime factors create different prime factorisations.
Reason (R): The prime factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion contradicts uniqueness apart from order, while the reason correctly states that principle.

activities.prompt: Explain why the prime factorisation is unique apart from the order of the factors.
activities.answer: Prime factorisation is unique apart from order because every composite number can be factorised as a product of primes, and any natural number can be written as a product of its prime factors. Prime factors may be repeated as many times as needed, so repeated copies remain part of the product. For 32760, the listed prime powers are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 13. Moving these factors into another order does not change the product or the prime factorisation. Thus, different arrangements may look different without giving different prime factorisations.
points: Explains that natural and composite numbers can be expressed using prime factors.
States that repeated prime factors may occur and remain in the product.
Uses 2, 3, 5, 7 and 13 as the listed prime powers for 32760.
Explains that only the arrangement, not the factorisation, changes.

activities.prompt: How does the prime factorisation method help the workshop find both the HCF and LCM of 6 and 20?
activities.answer: The workshop first factorises the composite numbers 6 and 20 into prime factors. Combining equal prime factors gives powers of primes, and once ascending order is fixed, the factorisation is unique. The prime factorisation method can then find both the HCF and the LCM. For these numbers, the HCF is 2. The LCM can be found from the HCF and the two integers. As a check, the HCF multiplied by the LCM should equal the product of 6 and 20. This is an application of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

lessons.title: Understanding polynomials and their degrees

activities.prompt: What makes a polynomial’s degree special?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet polynomial degrees
activities.body: The degree of a polynomial is the highest power of its variable. A degree-one polynomial is called linear. A degree-two polynomial is called quadratic. The word quadratic comes from quadrate, which means square. A degree-three polynomial is called cubic. A general cubic polynomial is written as ax3 + bx2 + cx + d. Its coefficients are real numbers, and its leading coefficient is not zero.
keyPoints: Degree means the highest power of the variable.
Degree one is linear, degree two is quadratic, and degree three is cubic.
A general cubic polynomial is ax3 + bx2 + cx + d.
activities.explanation: Degree helps us name and compare polynomials.

activities.prompt: In the quadratic polynomial 3x^2 + 5x + 4, what is the value of the leading coefficient?
steps: The polynomial is 3x^2 + 5x + 4.
The highest-power term is 3x^2, so its leading coefficient is 3.

activities.prompt: Can a polynomial’s zeroes tell us something special about its coefficients?

activities.title: Finding values and zeroes
activities.body: Start with p(x) = x² − 3x − 4. To find p(k), replace x with k. The value p(2) is −6, and p(0) is −4. Substituting x = −1 or x = 4 gives zero. A zero makes the polynomial’s value equal to zero. For a linear polynomial, solve ak + b = 0. Its zero depends on its number parts, called coefficients. The chapter asks about quadratic zeroes too.
keyPoints: Use p(k) for the value at x = k.
Replace x with k to work out the value.
A linear polynomial’s zero depends on its coefficients.

activities.body: A quadratic polynomial can be understood by factoring it and finding its zeroes. Begin with p(x) = 2x² − 8x + 6. Split the middle term, −8x, into two terms. Their product must be 12x². This gives (2x − 2)(x − 3), or 2(x − 1)(x − 3). Hence the zeroes are 1 and 3, and their product is 3.

activities.prompt: How many zeroes can a cubic hide, and how can we find them?

activities.title: Cubic polynomials and their zeroes
activities.body: A cubic polynomial can have at most three zeroes. The lesson looks at p(x) = 2x³ − 5x² − 14x + 8 and p(x) = 3x³ − 5x² − 11x − 3. For the second polynomial, 3 and −1 are zeroes. The calculations p(3) and p(−1) both end in zero. You will also use the rule for degree n.
keyPoints: A cubic polynomial has at most three zeroes.
The second polynomial takes 3 and −1 as zeroes.
A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.
activities.explanation: These rules help you check and summarise the zeroes.

activities.prompt: A game score is p(x)=3x³−5x²−11x−3. Inputs 3 and −1 both give zero score. Could one more zero exist?
steps: The calculation for p(3) ends in zero, so 3 is a zero.
For p(–1), the calculation ends in zero, so –1 is a zero.
This cubic already has two known zeroes.
Since the maximum is three, at most one more zero can exist.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How many zeroes can a cubic polynomial have at most?
options: Three
Two
Four
No limit
activities.explanation: A cubic polynomial can have at most three zeroes.

activities.prompt: A cubic polynomial can have at most ______ zeroes.
activities.hint: Think about the maximum for a cubic polynomial.
activities.explanation: The maximum number of zeroes of a cubic polynomial is three.

activities.prompt: The polynomial p(x) = 2x³ − 5x² − 14x + 8 is cubic.
activities.explanation: The lesson gives this polynomial as a cubic polynomial.

activities.prompt: Match each expression with its correct description.
activities.explanation: The first expression is cubic. The second polynomial takes 3 and −1 as zeroes.

3 and 1
3 and −3
3 and 2

options: p(3) and p(−1) both end in zero.
p(3) ends in zero, but p(−1) does not.
Neither p(3) nor p(−1) ends in zero.
p(3) ends in one, and p(−1) ends in two.
activities.explanation: Both calculations end in zero, matching the two stated zeroes.

options: Zero
One
Two
Three

why.Zero: Zero is wrong because two zeroes leave room for one more.
why.Two: Two is wrong because two are already known, not two extra.
why.Three: Three is wrong because three is the total limit, not extra count.

activities.explanation: One is right because a cubic has at most three zeroes.

No; a cubic must have exactly three zeroes.
Yes; four zeroes still fit a cubic.
Maybe; the polynomial's degree does not matter.

why.No; a cubic must have exactly three zero: This confuses a maximum with a required count.
This treats a cubic as if it allowed four zeroes.
why.Maybe; the polynomial's degree does not: This wrongly ignores the limit set by degree.

activities.explanation: No is right because a cubic has at most three zeroes.

No, because polynomials have no zeroes.
Yes, because each answer might be a zero.
Maybe, because the degree gives no limit.

This wrongly says polynomials cannot have zeroes.
why.Yes, because each answer might be a zero: This ignores the limit set by the degree.
why.Maybe, because the degree gives no limit: This wrongly treats the degree limit as uncertain.

activities.explanation: No is right because n zeroes already reach the limit.

activities.prompt: A game uses a cubic polynomial. A child says it always has exactly three zeroes. What reasoning shows the child's mistake?
options: At most three does not mean exactly three.
Three zeroes means one more is allowed.
A zero must make the polynomial equal one.
Every cubic has zeroes 3 and –1.

This confuses the maximum with the number already found.
why.A zero must make the polynomial equal on: This confuses zero with the value one.
This assumes one polynomial's zeroes belong to every cubic.

activities.explanation: This is right because ‘at most’ allows fewer than three.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between linear, quadratic, and cubic polynomials.
activities.answer: The difference is the degree, which is the highest power of the variable. A degree-one polynomial is called linear. A degree-two polynomial is called quadratic; the word quadratic comes from quadrate, meaning square. A degree-three polynomial is called cubic. A general cubic polynomial is written as ax3 + bx2 + cx + d. Its coefficients are real numbers, and its leading coefficient is not zero. These names identify polynomials according to their degrees.
points: Defines degree as the highest power of the variable.
Explains that degree one is linear and degree two is quadratic.
Explains that degree three is cubic.
States the general cubic form and its coefficient rule.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between finding the zero of a linear polynomial and finding the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial.
activities.answer: For a linear polynomial, find the single point where its straight-line graph meets the x-axis. The zero is the x-coordinate of that point, so a linear polynomial has exactly one zero. For a quadratic polynomial, its graph is a parabola. The zeroes are the x-coordinates where that parabola meets the x-axis. For example, for y = x² − 3x − 4, the zeroes are −1 and 4 because the parabola meets the x-axis there. Thus, a linear graph gives one zero, while the quadratic example gives two.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: introducing pairs of linear equations; consistent, inconsistent and dependent pairs; solving pairs graphically; the substitution method.

lessons.title: Introducing pairs of linear equations

activities.prompt: Could two simple clues reveal how many times Akhila enjoyed each game?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two quantities, two variables
activities.body: A linear equation in two variables shows how two quantities are linked. A variable is a letter standing for a number. Here, x means the number of Giant Wheel rides Akhila had. y means the number of times she played Hoopla. She played Hoopla half as many times. Her total spending was ₹20. The equation 3x + 4y = 20 represents this amount.
keyPoints: x represents Akhila's Giant Wheel rides.
y represents her Hoopla games.
A pair of equations represents the fair situation.
activities.explanation: Variables help us show how the two linked quantities fit together.

activities.title: Steer the straight line

tasks.say: Make the line flat.
tasks.then: A flat line has slope 0: y stays the same however x changes.

tasks.say: Make the line go downhill from left to right.
tasks.then: A negative slope means y falls as x grows.

tasks.say: Build y = 2x - 2: climb 2 for every 1 across, crossing the y-axis at -2.
tasks.then: You built y = 2x - 2.

activities.takeaway: m sets how steep the line is and c sets where it crosses the y-axis: y = mx + c.
activities.explanation: m sets how steep the line is and c sets where it crosses the y-axis: y = mx + c.

The total amount spent

activities.prompt: Akhila played Hoopla half as many times as she rode the Giant Wheel.
activities.explanation: This relationship helps us connect the numbers represented by x and y.

activities.prompt: Which equation represents the total amount spent?
activities.explanation: The equation 3x + 4y = 20 represents Akhila's total spending of ₹20.

activities.hint: This is the first variable used in the pair.

activities.explanation: Each pair connects a variable or equation with what it represents.

activities.prompt: Put these parts in order to show the total amount spent.
activities.explanation: Putting the parts together gives 3x + 4y = 20.

why.x + y = 20 and y = 2x: This counts fruit but ignores the different prices.
why.3x + 4y = 20 and x = y: This wrongly says both fruit counts are equal.

activities.explanation: This gives the spending and shows oranges are twice apples.

lessons.title: Consistent, inconsistent and dependent pairs

activities.prompt: What happens when two lines meet, stay apart, or overlap?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Pairs of linear equations
activities.body: Learn how pairs of linear equations are grouped. An inconsistent pair has no common solution. A consistent pair has a solution. Intersecting lines meet at one point and give a unique solution. Parallel lines do not meet, so they have no solution. Coincident lines lie on the same line. A dependent pair has infinitely many common solutions, and every dependent pair is consistent.
keyPoints: An inconsistent pair has no common solution.
A consistent pair has a solution.
A dependent pair has infinitely many common solutions and is consistent.
activities.explanation: These terms describe how the equations and their lines behave together.

activities.prompt: Two boxes contain 24 laddoos altogether. The first box has 4 more laddoos than the second box. How many laddoos are in the first box?
steps: Let x be the number in the first box and y the number in the second box.
The facts give x + y = 24 and x - y = 4.
Adding gives twice the first count as 28, so the first box has 14 laddoos.

lessons.title: The substitution method

activities.prompt: Ready to discover how replacing one variable can reveal whether two lines meet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How substitution works
activities.body: In substitution, you write one variable in terms of the other. You use the expression to reduce the pair to an equation in one variable. Then you substitute the first variable you found to find the other. The method is called substitution because one variable replaces another. Sometimes, a true statement without a variable means the pair has infinitely many solutions.
keyPoints: Write one variable in terms of the other.
Reduce the pair to an equation in one variable.
Substitute the first variable back to find the other.
activities.explanation: Each step helps you use one variable to find the other.

lessons.title: The elimination method

activities.prompt: Ready to make one variable disappear from two equations?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is elimination?
activities.body: Elimination means removing one variable from a pair of equations. You do this by making the coefficients of that variable numerically equal. The equal coefficients then let the variable cancel when one equation is subtracted from the other. The remaining one-variable equation gives the value of that variable. This method is called elimination because one variable is removed first.
keyPoints: Elimination removes one variable.
Equal coefficients let the chosen variable cancel.
One-variable equations give a variable's value.
activities.explanation: Equal coefficients make the chosen variable cancel.

activities.prompt: The income example has two equations. One is 9x – 4y = 2000. How can we remove y and find x?
steps: Multiply Equation (1) by 3 and Equation (2) by 4.
Their y coefficients are now equal, so y can cancel.
Subtract Equation (3) from Equation (4) to remove y.
The one-variable equation gives the value of x.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choosing what to eliminate
activities.body: When you use elimination, choose one variable to remove. Multiply both equations by suitable non-zero constants. This makes the coefficients of your chosen variable numerically equal. Subtract one new equation from the other so the chosen variable cancels. The resulting one-variable equation gives the value of that variable. A true statement without a variable means infinitely many solutions. A false statement without a variable means no solution.
keyPoints: Suitable non-zero constants make chosen coefficients equal.
The remaining equation gives the variable's value.
A final statement shows whether solutions exist.
activities.explanation: The final statement tells you whether solutions exist.

activities.prompt: What does the elimination method remove from a pair of equations?
options: One variable
Both variables
One constant
All terms
activities.explanation: Elimination removes one variable first. This is why the method has its name.

activities.prompt: Equal coefficients of y allow y to cancel.
activities.explanation: When the coefficients of y are equal, the variable y can cancel.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the method with its correct detail.
activities.explanation: The multipliers make the y coefficients equal. Subtracting then removes y.

activities.hint: This number is on the right-hand side.
activities.explanation: The given income equation is 9x − 4y = 2000.

options: Make chosen coefficients equal

activities.explanation: The multiplication makes the chosen variable's coefficients numerically equal. This helps the variable cancel.

activities.prompt: A false statement without a variable means the original pair has infinitely many solutions.
activities.explanation: A false statement without a variable means the original pair has no solution.

activities.prompt: Put the elimination steps in order.
items: Multiply Equation (1) by 3 and Equation (2) by 4

activities.explanation: The multiplication makes the y coefficients equal. Subtracting removes y and leaves one variable.

why.Subtraction works better with zero coeff: This believes subtraction can replace suitable non-zero multipliers.
why.Equal coefficients always require larger: This believes matching coefficients always makes equations larger.

activities.prompt: What happens when two lines meet, overlap, or run apart?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Pairs of linear equations
activities.body: Equations make two lines. Intersecting lines meet once. They give one unique solution. Such a pair is consistent. Coincident lines are the same line. Every point solves them, giving infinitely many. This pair is dependent and consistent. Parallel lines never meet, so their pair is inconsistent and has no solution. Substitution replaces one variable with an expression. Elimination removes one variable first. Some two-equation situations become linear pairs.
keyPoints: Intersecting: one unique solution and consistent
Coincident: infinitely many solutions, dependent and consistent
Parallel: no solution and inconsistent
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas for pairs of linear equations.

activities.prompt: Explain why the fair situation can be represented by a pair of linear equations in two variables.
activities.answer: The first equation, 3x + 4y = 20, describes the total amount Akhila spent on Giant Wheel rides and Hoopla games. The second equation, y = x/2, describes the relationship between the activities: her Hoopla count is half her Giant Wheel count. Together, these are two linear equations in the two variables x and y. They connect the numbers of rides and games with the total spending, so the fair situation can be represented by this pair.

Identifies y as the Hoopla count.
Explains the total-spending equation.

activities.context: Two route plans are shown as lines on a map. One pair crosses at a single point, so the plans have one shared solution. Another pair never meets, so it has no solution. A final pair lies on the same line, so it is dependent and consistent.
activities.prompt: If the second route pair is redrawn so that its lines meet at one point, what would happen?
options: The redrawn pair would have exactly one common solution.
The redrawn pair would have infinitely many common solutions.
The redrawn pair would continue to have no common solution.
The redrawn pair would become a coincident pair.

why.The redrawn pair would have infinitely m: Infinitely many solutions describe a dependent pair, not an intersecting pair.
why.The redrawn pair would continue to have: If the lines meet, they no longer form the parallel case.
why.The redrawn pair would become a coincide: A coincident pair requires the lines to lie on the same line.

activities.explanation: Meeting at one point makes the pair intersecting, which has a unique solution.

activities.context: Two route plans are shown as lines on a map. One pair crosses at a single point, so the plans have one shared solution. Another pair never meets, so it has no solution. A final pair lies on the same line, so it is dependent and consistent.
activities.prompt: What should the planner do if the final routes need exactly one common solution?
options: Change the arrangement so the lines meet at one point.
Keep both lines on the same line, because that gives one shared point.
Make the lines parallel, because separate lines give a common meeting point.
Leave the pair with no common solution, because having no solution makes it consistent.

why.Keep both lines on the same line, becaus: A coincident pair has infinitely many common solutions, not one.
why.Make the lines parallel, because separat: Parallel lines do not meet and have no solution.
why.Leave the pair with no common solution,: A pair with no solution is inconsistent, not consistent.

activities.explanation: Lines meeting at one point form an intersecting pair with a unique solution.

A is true but R is false.

activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the unique solution shows that a common solution exists.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A dependent pair is inconsistent.
Reason (R): A dependent pair has infinitely many common solutions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because dependent pairs have infinitely many common solutions, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an inconsistent pair and a dependent pair.
activities.answer: An inconsistent pair has no solution because the equations have no common solution. A dependent pair has infinitely many common solutions, so it is also consistent. The key difference is therefore the number of common solutions: none for an inconsistent pair and infinitely many for a dependent pair. The classifications are not opposites, since every dependent pair is consistent. A student should look for whether a common solution exists and whether the pair has infinitely many solutions when describing it.
points: An inconsistent pair has no solution.
An inconsistent pair has no common solution.
A dependent pair has infinitely many common solutions.
Every dependent pair is also consistent.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a clothing stall, Champa uses a graph display to compare two relations. One relation is y = 2x – 2, and her two lines intersect at (1, 0). In the first worked check, points are joined as lines AB and PQ; both pass through B at (6, 0), giving x = 6 and y = 0. In another check, multiplying makes two equations identical, so their lines coincide and allow infinitely many solutions. She finally chooses one pant and no skirt.

Solve once, plot the single point, and draw through it.

Solve twice and plot both pairs, but leave them separate.

why.Solve once, plot the single point, and d: One plotted point is not enough for this construction.
why.Draw the line first and then choose poin: The points should come from solutions before the line is formed.
why.Solve twice and plot both pairs, but lea: Plotting the points without joining them does not form the required line.

activities.prompt: Explain how the substitution method is used in the age situation involving Aftab and his daughter.
activities.answer: In the age situation, s and t represent Aftab and his daughter's ages. The expression s = 3t + 6 writes Aftab's age in terms of his daughter's age. To reduce the pair to an equation in one variable, use this expression to replace s in the other equation. After finding t, substitute its value back into s = 3t + 6 to find s. This is called substitution because one variable replaces another.

lessons.title: Introduction and History of Quadratic Equations

activities.prompt: How did people solve quadratic puzzles long before calculators?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What are quadratic equations?
activities.body: Equating a quadratic polynomial to zero gives a quadratic equation. Quadratic equations often arise in real-life situations. The prayer hall example connects its length, breadth and area with equations. Many people believe the Babylonians first solved them. Their method involved a positive sum and product. The history includes work by Euclid, Brahmagupta, Sridharacharya and Al-Khwarizmi. Indian mathematicians are often credited with the general form.
keyPoints: Equating a quadratic polynomial to zero gives a quadratic equation.
Prayer hall measurements lead to quadratic equations.
Different mathematicians contributed methods and formulas.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects quadratic equations with real life and their history.

activities.prompt: In cricket, two batters scored consecutive whole numbers of runs, and the product of their scores was 56. How many runs did the first batter score?
activities.explanation: The consecutive scores give x × (x + 1) = 56. This is the quadratic x² + x - 56 = 0. Its positive solution is 7, and 7 × (7 + 1) equals 56. Therefore the first batter scored 7 runs.
steps: The consecutive scores give x × (x + 1) = 56.
This is the quadratic x² + x - 56 = 0.
Its positive solution is 7, and 7 × (7 + 1) equals 56.
Therefore the first batter scored 7 runs.
activities.hint: Let the first score be x, so the second score is x plus one.

activities.prompt: What makes an equation quadratic, and how do real-life problems become one?

activities.title: What makes an equation quadratic?
activities.body: A quadratic equation has the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0. Here, a, b and c are real numbers, while a is not zero. If p(x) equals zero and p(x) has degree 2, the equation is quadratic. Write polynomial terms in descending order of degrees. The marble and toy examples help you form such equations.
keyPoints: The standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0.
The number a must not be zero.
Polynomial terms are written in descending order of degrees.
activities.explanation: These rules help you spot and form quadratic equations from the examples.

tasks.then: When the vertex sits on the x-axis there is exactly one root.

activities.prompt: A maker makes x toys. Each toy costs 55 minus x, and the total cost is 750. Which equation models this situation?
steps: Each toy costs 55 minus x. Therefore, x toys cost x(55 minus x).
The total cost is 750, so x(55 minus x) = 750.
Expanding and moving all terms gives x² – 55x + 750 = 0.
Thus, this is the standard quadratic equation for the toy count.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Connecting situations with quadratic equations
activities.body: John and Jivanti together had 45 marbles. Each of them lost 5 marbles. John's original number of marbles satisfies x² – 45x + 324 = 0. Each toy's cost was 55 minus the number of toys produced. The total cost was 750, so the number produced satisfies x² – 55x + 750 = 0.
keyPoints: John and Jivanti together had 45 marbles.
Each of them lost 5 marbles.
The toy count satisfies x² – 55x + 750 = 0.
activities.explanation: These examples connect each situation with its matching quadratic equation.

Rewrite it as 4x + 2 – 3x² = 0.

Rearranging does not change the signs of the terms.
The constant term stays positive when the terms are reordered.

The equation stays quadratic because its middle term has x.

lessons.title: Checking whether equations are quadratic

activities.prompt: Could an equation look quadratic but turn out not to be?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Simplify before deciding
activities.body: Checking an equation needs care. First simplify it. The second example looks quadratic. It simplifies to x + 12 = 0, a linear equation. It is not quadratic. The third example becomes x² + 3x − 1 = 0, so it is quadratic. The fourth example may look cubic because its left side contains x³. Yet it becomes 6x² + 12x + 12 = 0, so it is quadratic.
keyPoints: Simplify before deciding.
The second example becomes a linear equation.
The third and fourth examples are quadratic.
activities.explanation: Simplifying reveals the actual form before you decide.

activities.prompt: A student finds (x – 2)² + 1 = 2x – 3. Is it quadratic after checking?
steps: First, simplify the equation before deciding its kind.
Expanding and collecting terms gives x² – 6x + 8 = 0.
The simplified equation has x², so it is quadratic.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What should you do before deciding whether an equation is quadratic?
options: Simplify it before deciding.
Decide from its first appearance.
Treat every equation as quadratic.
Ignore the simplified form.
activities.explanation: Simplifying reveals the actual form before you decide.

activities.prompt: The second example may appear quadratic, but it is actually not quadratic.
activities.explanation: The second example may appear quadratic, but its simplified form is linear.

activities.prompt: The second example simplifies to the ______ equation x + 12 = 0.
activities.hint: This equation is not quadratic.
activities.explanation: The simplified equation is linear, so the example is not quadratic.

activities.prompt: What does the left side of the second example expand to?
options: x² + 3x − 1
x² + x + 8
x² − 6x + 8
activities.explanation: The left side of the second example expands to x² + x + 8.

activities.prompt: Match each example with its simplified form.
activities.explanation: The first, third, and fourth forms are quadratic. The second form is linear.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of the second example in order.
items: The left side expands to x² + x + 8.
The example is judged not quadratic.
activities.explanation: The second example first expands, then simplifies. Its final form is linear, so it is not quadratic.

activities.prompt: A student's equation has left side x² + x + 8. It simplifies to x + 12 = 0. Is it quadratic?
options: Yes, because the left side contains x².
No, because the simplified equation is linear.
Yes, because the equation has a constant term.

No, because a cubic term appears before simplifying.

why.No, because a cubic term appears before: It wrongly lets the unsimplified cubic term decide the kind.
why.Yes, because the first expansion has thr: It counts terms instead of checking the highest power.

activities.explanation: It is right because the final equation has x².

activities.prompt: A school club checks an equation that becomes x² + 3x – 1 = 0. Does it count as quadratic?

No, because it also contains an x term.

The second team, because its simplified equation has x².
Both teams, because each equation has a constant term.
Neither team, because their equations are not in one form.

why.The first team, because its original for: It checks the unsimplified first equation instead of the simplified one.
why.Both teams, because each equation has a: It wrongly thinks a constant term makes an equation quadratic.
why.Neither team, because their equations ar: It wrongly requires every quadratic equation to have one fixed form.

activities.explanation: It is right because the second simplified equation has x².

options: Only the first model, because x² appears in it.
Only the second model, because its simplified equation has x².
Both models, because x² appears somewhere in each.
Neither model, because the second model once looked cubic.

why.Only the first model, because x² appears: It trusts an appearance instead of checking the simplified equation.
why.Both models, because x² appears somewher: It wrongly counts an x² term before simplification.
why.Neither model, because the second model: It wrongly treats an earlier cubic-looking form as final.

lessons.title: Roots by factorisation

activities.prompt: What secret do the factors reveal about a quadratic’s roots?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Roots and factorisation
activities.body: A root is a real number that satisfies a quadratic equation. It is also called a solution. The zeroes of a quadratic polynomial are the roots of its quadratic equation. A quadratic equation can have at most two roots. We can factorise quadratic polynomials by splitting their middle terms. For example, –5x is split as –2x –3x in 2x² – 5x + 3. Then set each linear factor equal to zero to find the roots.
keyPoints: A root satisfies a quadratic equation.
A quadratic equation has at most two roots.
Set each linear factor equal to zero.
activities.explanation: Set linear factors to zero to find roots.

activities.prompt: On a school trip, x is the number of buses and (2x - 8)(2x - 18) = 0. What number of buses is given by the factor 2x - 18 = 0?
steps: The factor 2x - 18 must equal zero.
Then 2x = 18.
Dividing by 2 gives 9 buses.

gen.template: On a school trip, x is the number of buses and ({a}x - {b})({a}x - {c}) = 0. What number of buses is given by the factor {a}x - {c} = 0?

Then {a}x = {c}.
Dividing by {a} gives {answer} buses.
gen.hint: Set the factor involving the number of buses equal to zero.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A student must choose a root for 2x² − 3x + 1 = 0. How can a quick test show the choice?
steps: Try x = 1 because it is easy to replace.
Substituting gives 2(1)² − 3(1) + 1 = 0.
A number that satisfies the quadratic equation is a root.
So 1 is the root of this equation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which number is a root of 2x² – 3x + 1 = 0?
activities.explanation: Replacing x by 1 makes the left side zero, so 1 is a root.

activities.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a meaning given in this lesson.

activities.prompt: Which split matches the middle term of 2x² – 5x + 3?
activities.explanation: The middle term –5x is split as –2x –3x.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding roots in the correct order.
items: Set each linear factor equal to zero
activities.explanation: First split, then factorise, set factors to zero, and find the roots.

activities.prompt: A market stall's profit x in rupees satisfies x² - 8x + 7 = 0. What is the larger possible profit in rupees?
activities.explanation: The middle term -8x can be split as -x - 7x. Grouping gives (x - 1)(x - 7) = 0. The larger root comes from x - 7 = 0, so the profit is 7 rupees.
steps: The middle term -8x can be split as -x - 7x.
Grouping gives (x - 1)(x - 7) = 0.
The larger root comes from x - 7 = 0, so the profit is 7 rupees.

steps: Since x = 2 is a solution, split the middle term as -2x - 9x.
The constant 18 is twice 9, so grouping gives (x - 2)(x - 9) = 0.
Setting x - 9 = 0 gives 9 marbles.

The value is not a root because the left side stays negative.

lessons.title: The discriminant and the nature of roots

activities.prompt: Can one number reveal how many real roots a quadratic has?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What the discriminant tells you
activities.body: The discriminant is the part b² – 4ac of a quadratic equation. It tells you about its roots. If it is greater than zero, there are two distinct real roots. If it equals zero, there are two equal real roots. If it is less than zero, there are no real roots. You can use the quadratic formula to find the roots.
keyPoints: The discriminant is b² – 4ac.
Its size shows the nature of the roots.
The quadratic formula gives the roots of a quadratic equation.
activities.explanation: This gives you the main rule for this lesson.

activities.prompt: A quadratic equation has b² − 4ac greater than zero. Can it have just one real root?
steps: The expression b² − 4ac is the discriminant.
A discriminant greater than zero gives two distinct real roots.
Distinct roots are different, so they cannot be counted as one.
Therefore, the equation cannot have just one real root.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In 2x² – 4x + 3 = 0, what is the value of a?
activities.explanation: The coefficient of x² is 2, so a equals 2.

activities.prompt: The discriminant of 2x² – 4x + 3 = 0 is ______.
activities.hint: Use a = 2, b = –4 and c = 3.
activities.explanation: For this equation, b² – 4ac equals –8.

activities.prompt: The expression b² – 4ac is called the discriminant.
activities.explanation: This is the name given to b² – 4ac.

activities.prompt: Which root type does 2x² – 4x + 3 = 0 have?
options: two distinct real roots
two equal real roots
no real roots
four real roots
activities.explanation: Its discriminant is –8, which is less than zero.

activities.prompt: Order the discriminant cases from greater than zero to less than zero.
activities.explanation: These cases run from the greatest value to the smallest.

activities.prompt: Match each discriminant case with its root type.
activities.explanation: Each discriminant case has the root type shown here.

activities.prompt: A school puzzle uses a quadratic equation. Its discriminant is greater than zero. How many real roots can it have?
options: It has two distinct real roots.
It has two equal real roots.
It has no real roots.
It has exactly one real root.

You used the equal-roots rule, but the discriminant is greater than zero.
You used the less-than-zero rule, but the discriminant is greater than zero.
You counted two distinct roots as one root.

activities.explanation: Greater than zero gives two distinct real roots.

activities.prompt: In a maths club, 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0 has discriminant –8. What root result should the club record?
options: No real roots exist for this equation.
Two distinct real roots exist here.
Two equal real roots exist here.
One positive real root exists here.

You confused a negative discriminant with a positive one.
You used the zero-discriminant rule, but the discriminant is –8.
You assumed one root without checking the negative discriminant.

activities.explanation: A negative discriminant means the equation has no real roots.

activities.prompt: A homework equation is 3x² − 2x + 1/3 = 0. Its discriminant equals zero. What root result should the student record?
options: Two equal real roots exist here.
Two distinct real roots exist here.
No real roots exist for this equation.
One positive real root exists here.

Greater than zero gives distinct roots, not equal ones.
Less than zero gives no real roots, not equal roots.
You assumed a positive root without checking the zero discriminant.

activities.explanation: Two equal real roots occur when the discriminant equals zero.

activities.prompt: A student says 2x² − 4x + 3 = 0 has real roots because the quadratic formula gives roots. What correction explains the flaw?
options: The discriminant is –8, so there are no real roots.
The discriminant is zero, so there are equal real roots.
The formula gives roots, so they must always be real.
The equation is not quadratic, so the formula cannot work.

why.The discriminant is zero, so there are e: Zero would give equal real roots, but this discriminant is –8.
why.The formula gives roots, so they must al: You thought the quadratic formula always gives real roots.
why.The equation is not quadratic, so the fo: You ignored the given quadratic equation and its discriminant.

activities.explanation: gives –8, and a negative discriminant means no real roots.

options: No real square can equal that negative value.
A zero real square can equal that negative value.
Two equal real squares can equal that negative value.
One positive real square can equal that negative value.

why.A zero real square can equal that negati: You confused zero with a negative value.
why.Two equal real squares can equal that ne: You assumed equal squares could still be negative.
why.One positive real square can equal that: You assumed a positive square could equal a negative value.

Greater than zero gives two distinct real roots, not equal roots.
Less than zero gives no real roots, not equal roots.
Negative eight belongs to the other given equation.

activities.explanation: Two equal real roots occur when the discriminant equals zero.

lessons.title: Applying the quadratic formula and summarising

activities.prompt: Can we discover the perfect spot for the pole in the park?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Finding the pole's distance
activities.body: The park's diameter is 13 metres. Start with the quadratic equation x² + 7x − 60 = 0. The discriminant is b² − 4ac. Here, it is 289, which is greater than zero. The quadratic formula gives x = 5 or x = –12. Ignore –12 because a distance must be positive. The pole is 5 metres from gate B and 12 metres from gate A.
keyPoints: The discriminant is b² − 4ac.
The quadratic formula can be used when b² − 4ac is at least zero.
A distance cannot be negative.
activities.explanation: This card summarises the formula method and the valid pole distance.

activities.prompt: A pole must stand on a circular park’s edge. How far is it from each gate?
steps: The pole must stand on the boundary; the diameter is 13 metres.
B is x metres away; A is x + 7 metres away.
Therefore, Pythagoras gives (x + 7)² + x² = 13², then x² + 7x − 60 = 0.
Roots are 5 and −12. Positive 5 works: B is 5 metres and A is 12 metres.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Roots and zeroes
activities.body: A root is a value that makes a quadratic equation equal to zero. The zeroes of a quadratic polynomial are the same as its equation's roots. Roots can be found by equating each factor of a factorised quadratic polynomial to zero. The pole formula gives x = 5 and x = –12. Ignore –12, because a distance must be positive. Keep x = 5.
keyPoints: A root makes a quadratic equation equal to zero.
Polynomial zeroes and equation roots are the same.
Each factor can be equated to zero.
activities.explanation: This card connects roots, zeroes and factorised quadratics.

activities.prompt: Which equation comes from Pythagoras for the pole?
options: (x + 7)² + x² = 5²
activities.explanation: Pythagoras adds the squares of the gate distances. These distances are x and x + 7.

activities.prompt: The discriminant of x² + 7x − 60 = 0 is ______.
activities.hint: It is greater than zero.
activities.explanation: The pole equation has discriminant 289. It is greater than zero, so the quadratic formula can be used.

activities.prompt: Which value is the pole's distance from gate B?
options: 12 metres
5 metres
–12 metres
7 metres
activities.explanation: The valid value is x = 5. This places the pole 5 metres from gate B.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its result in the pole problem.
activities.explanation: The discriminant is 289. The formula gives x = 5 or x = –12. Only 5 is a valid distance.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for finding the pole's distance in order.
items: Use the formula to get x = 5 or x = –12.
Ignore –12 because a distance must be positive.
Record 5 metres from gate B and 12 metres from gate A.
activities.explanation: The equation comes from Pythagoras. The discriminant checks the formula, and only the positive distance is kept.

activities.prompt: Why can the quadratic formula be used for the pole equation?
options: The discriminant is zero.
The discriminant is negative.
The equation has no roots.
b² − 4ac is positive.
activities.explanation: The formula can be used when b² − 4ac is at least zero. Here, it is 289, so this condition is met.

activities.prompt: A bus passenger model is P(x) = (x - 6)(x - 10), where x is the passenger count. If the bus can carry fewer than 10 passengers, which zero x of P(x) is allowed?
activities.explanation: Equating the two factors to zero gives the zeroes 6 and 10. The first zero is fewer than 10 passengers, while the second is not. The allowed zero is 6 passengers.
steps: Equating the two factors to zero gives the zeroes 6 and 10.
The first zero is fewer than 10 passengers, while the second is not.
The allowed zero is 6 passengers.
activities.hint: First equate both factors to zero, then use the passenger limit.

It gives one repeated root.

The quadratic formula cannot be used.

This mistake treats a positive discriminant as if it were zero.
This mistake ignores the positive root 5.
This mistake thinks the formula requires a zero discriminant.

activities.prompt: A rectangular playground has area 60 square metres. Its sides are x metres and x + 7 metres. Which equation finds a possible side length?

why.x(x + 7) = −60: Two side lengths cannot have a negative product.
why.x(x − 7) = 60: The second side is x + 7, not x − 7.

options: Use 5; the sides are 5 metres and 12 metres.
Use −12; the sides are −12 metres and −5 metres.
Use both roots; one playground side may be negative.
Use neither root; the quadratic formula gives no usable values.

why.Use −12; the sides are −12 metres and −5: This wrongly chooses a negative root for a side length.
why.Use both roots; one playground side may: This confuses equation roots with possible playground sides.

activities.prompt: A pole is on the boundary of a circular park with diameter 13 metres. Its gate distances are x metres and x + 7 metres. Which equation follows from Pythagoras?
options: x² + 7² = 13²

why.(x + 7)² + x² = 13: This forgets that the 13-metre diameter must also be squared.
why.(x + 7)² − x² = 13²: This subtracts the squared distances instead of adding them.

activities.prompt:

activities.prompt: Explain why the prayer hall example gives a quadratic equation and how to form the equation that determines its breadth.
activities.answer: The area relation is 2x² + x = 300, where x represents the breadth. Because the length is one metre more than twice the breadth, 2x² + x describes the area of the hall. Moving 300 to the left side produces 2x² + x – 300 = 0. This is a quadratic equation because a quadratic polynomial has been equated to zero. The breadth can then be found by solving this equation, after which the length can be found from the stated relation.
points: Identifies x as the breadth.
Explains the area expression 2x² + x.
Shows how subtracting 300 produces the quadratic equation.
Explains that the breadth is found by solving the equation.

activities.context: John and Jivanti together had 45 marbles, and each of them lost 5 marbles. John’s original number of marbles satisfies a quadratic equation. In a toy-producing situation, the cost of producing each toy was 55 minus the number of toys produced, and the total cost was 750. The number of toys produced also satisfies a quadratic equation.
activities.prompt: When the toy equation is written with its terms in descending order of degree, what should come first?
options: The term containing the square of x
The term containing x
The constant term
Whichever term the writer places first

why.The term containing x: The linear term has a lower degree than the squared term.
why.The constant term: The constant term has the lowest degree.
why.Whichever term the writer places first: The order is fixed by the degrees, not chosen freely.

activities.explanation: Terms must be arranged from highest degree to lowest degree.

activities.context: John and Jivanti together had 45 marbles, and each of them lost 5 marbles. John’s original number of marbles satisfies a quadratic equation. The original total plus the losses of both children equals the remaining total.
The original total minus one child’s loss equals the remaining total.
One child’s loss minus the original total equals the remaining total.

why.The original total plus the losses of bo: Losses reduce the original total rather than increase it.
why.The original total minus one child’s los: Both children lose marbles, not only one.
why.One child’s loss minus the original tota: The remaining total is not found by subtracting the total from the loss.

activities.explanation: Both children lose marbles, so both losses are subtracted.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): John’s marble equation is quadratic.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion contradicts the nonzero requirement, while the reason states that requirement.

activities.prompt: Explain why x² – 55x + 750 = 0 is a quadratic equation and why it is in standard form.
activities.answer: The equation x² – 55x + 750 = 0 is quadratic because the unknown x has degree 2: it appears as x². It is also in standard form, ax² + bx + c = 0. The terms are arranged in descending order of degree, so the squared term comes first, the linear term comes next, and the constant term comes last. Its leading coefficient is not zero, and the coefficients are real numbers.
points: Identifies x² as a degree-2 term
Uses the form ax² + bx + c = 0
Places terms in descending order of degree
Notes that the leading coefficient is nonzero

activities.context: At school, a student is preparing notes on checking whether equations are quadratic. The notes show (x – 2)² + 1 = 2x – 3, a second example with left side x² + x + 8, a third example, and a fourth example. Other tasks state that a rectangular plot has area 528 square metres, two consecutive positive integers have product 306, and a train travels 480 kilometres at a uniform speed. The student will simplify equations before classifying them.
activities.prompt: After simplifying the first equation, how should the student classify it?
options: It is quadratic because it becomes x² – 6x + 8 = 0.
It is linear because the squared expression is on the left.
It is cubic because (x – 2)² contains a square.
It cannot be classified until the equation is expanded.

why.It is linear because the squared express: The position of the squared expression does not determine the final classification.
why.It is cubic because (x – 2)² contains a: A squared expression does not make an equation cubic.
why.It cannot be classified until the equati: Expanding alone is not enough; the whole equation must be simplified.

activities.explanation: The simplified equation is x² – 6x + 8 = 0, so it is quadratic.

activities.context: At school, a student is preparing notes on checking whether equations are quadratic. The notes show (x – 2)² + 1 = 2x – 3, a second example with left side x² + x + 8, a third example, and a fourth example. Other tasks state that a rectangular plot has area 528 square metres, two consecutive positive integers have product 306, and a train travels 480 kilometres at a uniform speed. The student will simplify equations before classifying them.
activities.prompt: If the smaller of the two consecutive positive integers is x, which setup correctly represents their product of 306?

why.x² = 306: x² represents the product of two equal integers, not consecutive ones.
why.x(x + 2) = 306: x + 2 is not the next consecutive integer after x.
why.2(x + 1) = 306: The expression 2(x + 1) represents a sum-related calculation rather than their product.

activities.explanation: The two consecutive integers are x and x + 1, so their product is x(x + 1).

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The second example is not a quadratic equation.
Reason (R): It simplifies to the linear equation x + 12 = 0.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains the classification because the simplified equation is linear.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The fourth example is cubic because its left side expands to x³ + 6x² + 12x + 8.
Reason (R): The fourth example may appear cubic even though it is actually quadratic.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The claim is false because the fourth example becomes 6x² + 12x + 12 = 0, while the reason correctly notes its misleading cubic appearance.

activities.prompt: Explain why the second example and the third example are classified differently.
activities.answer: The second example and the third example are classified differently after simplification. The left side of the second example expands to x² + x + 8, but the whole equation simplifies to x + 12 = 0. Since this is linear, the second example is not quadratic. The third example becomes x² + 3x – 1 = 0, so it is quadratic. This shows why an equation should be simplified before deciding: seeing x² in an intermediate expression does not by itself make the final equation quadratic.
points: The second left side expands to x² + x + 8.
The second example simplifies to the linear equation x + 12 = 0.
The third example becomes x² + 3x – 1 = 0 and is quadratic.
Equations should be simplified before they are classified.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school activity, learners prepare cards showing quadratic equations solved by factorisation. A card tests 2x² – 3x + 1 by replacing x with 1; the left side becomes zero, so 1 is recorded as a root, also called a solution. Another card splits the middle term of 2x² – 5x + 3 as –2x – 3x. A further card notes a repeated factor in 3x² – 6x + 2 and records the same root for each repeated factor.
activities.prompt: What does the result of replacing x with 1 show on the first card?
options: The number satisfies the quadratic equation.
It proves that x must always be replaced by 1.
It shows that 1 is the only possible value of x.
It shows that factorisation cannot be used.

why.It proves that x must always be replaced: The substitution checks one value; it does not require that value to replace x always.
why.It shows that 1 is the only possible val: Finding one root does not show that other values cannot be roots.
why.It shows that factorisation cannot be us: A quadratic polynomial can be factorised by splitting its middle term.

activities.explanation: A root is a real number that satisfies the quadratic equation.

activities.context: At a school activity, learners prepare cards showing quadratic equations solved by factorisation. A card tests 2x² – 3x + 1 by replacing x with 1; the left side becomes zero, so 1 is recorded as a root, also called a solution. Another card splits the middle term of 2x² – 5x + 3 as –2x – 3x. A further card notes a repeated factor in 3x² – 6x + 2 and records the same root for each repeated factor.
activities.prompt: What should the learner do about the repeated factor on the further card?
options: Record its root once for every occurrence of that factor.
Assign a different root to each occurrence.
Record the root only once, no matter how often the factor appears.
Replace the repeated factor with a middle-term split.

why.Assign a different root to each occurren: A repeated factor does not change the root into different roots.
why.Record the root only once, no matter how: The repetition must be represented for every occurrence of the factor.
why.Replace the repeated factor with a middl: A repeated factor is handled by repeating the root, not by splitting a middle term.

activities.explanation: In 3x² – 6x + 2 = 0, the root is repeated for each repeated factor.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If replacing x by 1 makes the left side zero, then 1 is a root of 2x² – 3x + 1 = 0.
Reason (R): The left side of that equation becomes zero when x is replaced by 1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason gives the substitution result that establishes that 1 satisfies the equation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The zeroes of 2x² – 5x + 3 are the roots of 2x² – 5x + 3 = 0.
Reason (R): The middle term –5x can be split as –2x –3x.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the middle-term split assists factorisation rather than explaining why zeroes and roots are the same.

activities.prompt: Explain why replacing x by 1 shows that 1 is a root, and describe how factorisation is used to find roots.
activities.answer: Replacing x by 1 in 2x² – 3x + 1 makes the left side equal to zero. Therefore, 1 satisfies the quadratic equation and is a root, also called a solution. To find roots by factorisation, split the middle term into terms that allow the polynomial to be written as linear factors. Set each linear factor equal to zero because the roots are found this way. The zeroes of the quadratic polynomial are the same as the roots of its quadratic equation.
points: Substitution makes the left side zero.
A number satisfying the equation is a root or solution.
Splitting the middle term assists factorisation.
Each linear factor is set equal to zero.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.1: Patterns in Daily Life

activities.prompt: Where can we spot patterns in nature, money, and family life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Patterns Around You
activities.body: Patterns appear in nature and daily life. Sunflower petals and honeycomb holes show patterns. Salaries can rise by a fixed amount each year. Ladder rungs can shrink by a fixed amount each time. Savings can also change over time. Rabbit-pair numbers can grow in a repeating pattern. Look at each sequence and ask what changes.
keyPoints: Natural patterns include sunflower petals and honeycomb holes.
Daily-life sequences can change in regular ways.
Ask what changes from one term to the next.
activities.explanation: Finding the rule helps you understand each pattern.

activities.prompt: A sunflower has 5 rings, with 5 petals in each ring. How many petals does it have altogether?
steps: There are 5 rings and 5 petals in each ring.
Equal groups are added by multiplication, so use 5 groups of 5 petals.
5 x 5 = 25 petals.

activities.title: Meet Arithmetic Progressions
activities.body: An arithmetic progression is a list. Each term comes from adding one fixed number to the term before it. That fixed number is the common difference. A positive difference makes terms increase. A negative difference makes them decrease. A zero difference keeps them the same. Consecutive terms have equal differences. The first term is a1, the second is a2, and the nth term is an.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.3: Finite APs, Infinite APs and Finding the Common Difference

activities.prompt: What if a pattern could keep going forever without ever ending?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Arithmetic Progressions
activities.body: An arithmetic progression, or AP, is a list of terms. Each term is found by adding the same common difference. The first term is called a. A finite AP has a limited number of terms and a last term. An infinite AP continues without a last term. To find d, subtract a term from the term immediately after it.
keyPoints: Finite APs have a last term.
Infinite APs have no last term.
Find d by subtracting a term from the next term.
activities.explanation: You can now recognise AP types and find their common difference.

activities.prompt: An AP starts with 4 rupees and has a common difference of 6 rupees. What is the second term in rupees?
steps: The first term is 4 rupees and the common difference is 6 rupees.
Add the common difference to the first term: 10 = 4 + 6.
The second term is 10 rupees.

Add the common difference to the first term: {next_term} = {a} + {d}.
The second term is {answer} rupees.
gen.hint: Add the common difference to the first term.
wrongWhy: You subtracted the first term instead of adding the common difference.
You multiplied the two values instead of adding the common difference.
You subtracted the common difference instead of adding it.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.title: Build the progression

tasks.say: Make every term the same.
tasks.then: With d = 0 the progression never changes.

tasks.say: Make the terms go down.
tasks.then: A negative common difference makes each term smaller.

tasks.say: Make the 10th term 29.
tasks.then: The 10th term is a + 9d, and here that is 29.

activities.takeaway: Each term adds the same difference d; the nth term is a + (n - 1)d.
activities.explanation: Each term adds the same difference d; the nth term is a + (n - 1)d.

activities.prompt: A toy machine starts at value a. It adds the same amount d each turn. Can we predict every later value?
steps: Start with a because it is the first value.
Add d each turn because it is the common difference.
Keep adding d because this same rule builds the AP.
So knowing a and d lets us list every later term.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Two consecutive terms of an AP are 8 marbles and 11 marbles. What is the common difference in marbles?
activities.explanation: The earlier consecutive term is 8 marbles and the next term is 11 marbles. Subtract the earlier term from the next term: 3 = 11 - 8. The common difference is 3 marbles.
steps: The earlier consecutive term is 8 marbles and the next term is 11 marbles.
Subtract the earlier term from the next term: 3 = 11 - 8.
The common difference is 3 marbles.
activities.hint: Subtract the earlier term from the term immediately after it.

The previous term is 10 cm.
activities.hint: Move backward by one common difference.

activities.prompt: How can you quickly find any term in an arithmetic pattern?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Finding any term of an AP
activities.body: In an AP, the first term is a and the common difference is d. The second, third and fourth terms are a + d, a + 2d and a + 3d. The nth term follows this pattern: a + (n – 1)d. This formula is also written as an = a + (n – 1)d. The nth term is called the general term. With m terms, am is the last term.
keyPoints: The second term is a + d.
The nth term is a + (n – 1)d.
The nth term is also called the general term.
activities.explanation: Replace n with the term number and subtract 1 from it.

activities.prompt: An arithmetic progression has first term 4 and common difference 2. What is its second term?
steps: The first term is 4.
The second term is found by adding one common difference 2.

gen.hint: Add the common difference {d} to the first term {a}.

activities.title: Build the progression

tasks.say: Make every term the same.
tasks.then: With d = 0 the progression never changes.

tasks.say: Make the terms go down.
tasks.then: A negative common difference makes each term smaller.

tasks.say: Make the 10th term 29.
tasks.then: The 10th term is a + 9d, and here that is 29.

activities.takeaway: Each term adds the same difference d; the nth term is a + (n - 1)d.
activities.explanation: Each term adds the same difference d; the nth term is a + (n - 1)d.

activities.prompt: A game shows the scores 2, 7, 12 and so on. What is the 10th score?
steps: The first score is 2 because the game starts with 2.
The common difference is 5 because each next score rises by 5.
The formula adds d for each step before the 10th term.
So a + (10 – 1)d gives the 10th score, 47.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.explanation: The first term is 4 and the common difference is 4. The last term comes after 5 - 1 additions of the common difference. 4 + (5 - 1) x 4 = 20.

The last term comes after 5 - 1 additions of the common difference.
activities.hint: Add 5 - 1 common differences to the first term 4.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.5: The Sum of the First n Terms

activities.prompt: Could Gauss find a shortcut for adding all the numbers from 1 to 100?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Adding Numbers with Gauss’s Method
activities.body: This lesson uses sums to make repeated additions quicker. Gauss added the integers from 1 to 100 by reversing their order. Each pair had the same sum of 101. Adding the forward and reverse arrangements gave twice the original sum. The chapter also gives a formula for sums of the first n terms. Its four quantities are S, a, d and n.
keyPoints: Gauss paired numbers with the same sum.
Each pair had a sum of 101.
The sum formula uses S, a, d and n.
activities.explanation: Pairing equal sums makes a long sum easier to handle.

activities.prompt: What is the sum of the whole numbers from 1 to 20?
steps: The whole numbers run from 1 to 20.
Gauss's pairing gives the sum as 20 x (20 + 1) divided by 2.
Therefore, the sum is 210.

This leaves exactly the sum of the first 20 terms.

lessons.title: Lesson 5.6: Chapter Summary

activities.prompt: How can you uncover a number pattern and predict what comes next?

activities.title: Chapter Summary
activities.body: An arithmetic progression is a list of numbers. Each new term follows one rule. You add the same d for every next term. This is the common difference. Consecutive differences must be equal. The nth term uses a + (n – 1)d. A finite list has a last term, l. Its sum uses n, a and l. In an AP, b is the average of a and c.
keyPoints: Each new term adds the common difference d.
The nth term is an = a + (n – 1)d.
If a, b and c are in AP, b is the arithmetic mean of a and c.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect the rule, the formula and the total sum.

The common difference is 2.

activities.prompt: How does the nth-term formula help find the tenth term of the AP 2, 7, 12 and so on?
activities.answer: The nth-term formula gives any term of an arithmetic progression without listing all earlier terms. For the progression 2, 7, 12 and so on, the first term is a = 2 and the common difference is d = 5. For the tenth term, put n = 10 in an = a + (n – 1)d. This gives an = 2 + (10 – 1)5 = 47. The same method explains why the tenth term is 47. It also shows why the position is reduced by one: the first term already accounts for one term.
points: Identifies a = 2 and d = 5.
Uses n = 10 in an = a + (n – 1)d.
Calculates the term as 2 + (10 – 1)5.
Explains that 47 is the tenth term.

activities.title: Rules for Similar Polygons
activities.body: Similar polygons have equal corresponding angles. Their corresponding sides stay in the same ratio. This common ratio is the scale factor. It is also called the Representative Fraction. Maps and blueprints use a suitable scale factor. A shadow is an enlargement because light travels in straight lines. A polygon and its shadow keep the same shape, but their sizes differ.

activities.title: Understanding Similar Triangles
activities.body: A triangle is also a polygon. Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles. Their corresponding sides are in the same ratio. Triangles with equal corresponding angles are called equiangular triangles. In two equiangular triangles, the ratio of any corresponding sides is always the same. A line parallel to one side divides the other two sides in the same ratio. The converse is also true.

Corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
A parallel line divides two sides in the same ratio.
