activities.title: Using parallel-line theorems
activities.body: Parallel-line theorems help you solve geometry questions. Lines parallel to the same line are parallel to each other. Alternate angles can show that two angles are equal. activities.title: Understanding SAS Similarity
activities.body: SAS similarity compares two triangles. First, one angle in one triangle must equal one angle in the other. Second, the two sides including these equal angles must be proportional. Proportional means matching side pairs have the same ratio. SAS means Side–Angle–Side similarity.
keyPoints: One angle in each triangle must be equal.
The two included sides must be proportional.
SAS means Side–Angle–Side similarity.
activities.explanation: SAS checks equal angles and proportional included sides.

activities.prompt: Two triangles have equal included angles, and the sides around those angles are proportional. A side in the first triangle is 3 cm and its matching side in the second triangle is 6 cm. What is the scale factor from the first triangle to the second?
steps: The equal included angles and proportional surrounding sides give SAS similarity.
The scale factor is the matching side in the second triangle divided by the matching side in the first.
So the scale factor is 2.

Therefore, the triangles are similar by the SAS Similarity Criterion.

activities.context: A student has two photographs of the same monument in different sizes. The student plans to use the photographs to find the monument's height indirectly and to compare corresponding angles. If the photographs were instead the same size but had been taken at different ages, the student would need to reconsider whether they could be treated as similar figures.
activities.prompt: What should the student expect when comparing corresponding angles in the two photographs?
options: The corresponding angles remain equal.
The corresponding angles become unequal because the photographs have different sizes.
The corresponding angles are equal only if the photographs are congruent.
The corresponding angles depend on which photograph is larger.

why.The corresponding angles become unequal: Different sizes do not change the equality of these angles.
why.The corresponding angles are equal only: The photographs have different sizes and are therefore not congruent.
why.The corresponding angles depend on which: The angles are equal for both photographs, regardless of which is larger.

activities.explanation: Corresponding angles in photographs of different sizes are equal.

activities.context: A student has two photographs of the same monument in different sizes. why.They would be similar because they have: Having the same size does not make this particular pair similar.
why.They would be similar because they show: Showing the same monument is enough for photographs of different sizes, but not for this pair.

activities.explanation: Photographs of the same size taken at different ages are not similar.

activities.prompt:

Reason (R): They show the same monument, and photographs of the same monument in different sizes are similar.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly applies the rule about photographs of the same monument in different sizes.

activities.prompt:

A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Similarity explains their common shape but does not explain why their different sizes prevent congruence.

activities.prompt: Explain why photographs of the same monument in different sizes are similar, but photographs of the same size taken at different ages are not similar.
activities.answer: Photographs of the same monument in different sizes are similar because they show the same monument, and photographs of the same monument in different sizes are similar. Similar figures have the same shape but need not have the same size, so using different sizes is allowed. Photographs of the same size taken at different ages are covered by a different rule: they are not similar. Therefore, equal size alone cannot be used to claim similarity for that pair. The student must use the rule that matches how the photographs were taken.
points: Uses the rule for photographs of the same monument in different sizes
Explains that different sizes are allowed for similar figures
Uses the rule for same-size photographs taken at different ages
Does not treat equal size alone as proof of similarity

The sign and its shadow have the same shape but different sizes, so their corresponding sides are in the same ratio and their corresponding angles are equal. A drafter later prepares a building blueprint using a suitable scale factor so that the drawing has the same shape as the actual outline.
activities.prompt: If the student traces a larger shadow of the same sign, what would remain unchanged?

The shape would stay the same, but corresponding angles would become unequal.

The shape would change because the shadow would be larger.

A is true but R is false.

activities.prompt: Explain how the straight-line travel of light explains why a shadow can be treated as an enlargement, and what remains unchanged.
activities.answer: Light travels in straight lines, so a shadow is an enlargement of the object that casts it. An enlargement changes the size but keeps the same shape. Therefore, a polygon and its shadow have equal corresponding angles and corresponding sides that are in the same ratio. They are similar polygons. The scale factor is the common ratio of those sides, and it is also called the Representative Fraction.

A shadow is an enlargement.
The shape and corresponding angles remain unchanged.
Corresponding sides are in the same ratio.

activities.prompt: Explain how the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem is used in the construction.
activities.answer: The converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem says that if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then it is parallel to the third side. This equal-area result supports the argument that the dividing line is parallel to the third side.

activities.title: Building the distance rule
activities.body: Find the distance between two points by finding their horizontal and vertical differences. Square these differences, then add them. Take only the positive square root of this sum. This rule is called the distance formula. Pythagoras theorem helps when points do not lie on a coordinate axis, including points in different quadrants.
keyPoints: The coordinate differences are x2 – x1 and y2 – y1.
This rule is called the distance formula.
Only the positive square root is used because distance is never negative.
activities.explanation: These steps join coordinate differences with Pythagoras theorem to find distance.

gen.hint: Subtract the smaller x-coordinate from the larger x-coordinate.

activities.title: Formula summary
activities.body: The distance formula finds the distance between P and Q. A special formula finds a point's distance from the origin. You will also use the mid-point and section formulas. External division concerns the line segment joining A and B. The note to the reader says it is for higher classes. Try choosing the right formula for each task.
keyPoints: The distance formula gives the distance between P and Q.
The special distance formula gives a point's distance from the origin.
The mid-point and section formulas use coordinate sums.
External division is studied in higher classes.
activities.explanation: The lesson links each method to its main use.

activities.prompt: P is the point (2, 3) and Q is the point (5, 7). What is the distance from P to Q in cm?
steps: P is (2, 3) and Q is (5, 7).
The coordinate changes are 3 and 4, so the squared distance is 25 = 3*3 + 4*4.
Taking the square root gives 5 = sqrt(25).
Therefore, the distance from P to Q is 5 cm.

activities.prompt: Shops A and B lie on one path. Point P divides AB internally, with PA : PB = m1 : m2. How can we find P?
steps: Start with PA : PB = m1 : m2, because P divides AB internally.
Use x = (m1x2 + m2x1)/(m1 + m2) because P needs an x-coordinate.
Use y = (m1y2 + m2y1)/(m1 + m2) because P needs a y-coordinate.
Both coordinates together give the complete position of P.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Explain how a pair of coordinate axes helps to locate a point, and state how its x- and y-coordinates are identified.
activities.answer: A pair of coordinate axes provides the reference lines needed to locate a point. The point’s x-coordinate, also called the abscissa, is its distance from the y-axis. Its y-coordinate, also called the ordinate, is its distance from the x-axis. Together, these coordinate values identify the point’s position in the graph. Points on the x-axis have the form (x, 0), while points on the y-axis have the form (0, y).
points: A pair of coordinate axes is needed.
The x-coordinate is distance from the y-axis.
The x-coordinate is called the abscissa.
The y-coordinate is distance from the x-axis and is called the ordinate.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain how the distance rule is built from the horizontal and vertical coordinate differences.
activities.answer: The rule begins by finding the horizontal difference, RS = x2 – x1, and the vertical difference, QT = y2 – y1. For R(4, 0) and S(6, 0), the horizontal difference is 2 units, so their distance is 2 units. For C(0, 3) and D(0, 8), the vertical difference is 5 units, so their distance is 5 units. When the points do not lie on a coordinate axis, Pythagoras theorem is used to find the distance. The same theorem is used for points in different quadrants. This rule is called the distance formula.
points: Finds the horizontal difference as x2 – x1
Finds the vertical difference as y2 – y1
Uses Pythagoras theorem when needed
Names the rule as the distance formula

activities.prompt: How does the section formula locate points on a line segment, and how can a mid-point or trisection point be found?
activities.answer: The section formula is used when a point divides a segment in a stated ratio. For the segment with endpoints (4, –3) and (8, 5), applying it for the ratio 3 : 1 gives (7, 3). For a mid-point, the division ratio is 1 : 1, so the same rule gives the coordinates of the mid-point of a join. For trisection, the two chosen points must satisfy AP = PQ = QB. The first of these points is obtained by applying the section formula, and the second is then found from the section formula.

activities.prompt: Explain how the internal section formula and the mid-point formula differ, and how external division is treated.
activities.answer: The internal section formula is used for the stated internal ratio PA : PB = m1 : m2. Its x-coordinate is (m1 x2 + m2 x1)/(m1 + m2), and its y-coordinate is (m1 y2 + m2 y1)/(m1 + m2). The mid-point formula is different because it uses x1 + x2 and y1 + y2 as its coordinate sums. External division is treated separately. The Section Formula for external division will be studied in higher classes, so the internal section formula should not be presented as the external-division method.
points: Identifies the internal ratio PA : PB = m1 : m2
Gives the correct x-coordinate formula
Gives the correct y-coordinate formula

chapters.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
chapters.summary: In this chapter: lesson 1: what trigonometry is for; lesson 2: the six trigonometric ratios; lesson 3: history and size independence of trigonometric ratios; lesson 4: finding values for 45°, 30° and 60°.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What Trigonometry Is For

activities.prompt: How can triangles help us measure things we cannot reach?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Trigonometry helps us measure
activities.body: Trigonometry helps us solve problems with right-angled triangles. These triangles appear in real-life situations, such as finding a river's width, a balloon's altitude, or the top of Qutub Minar. It studies how the sides and angles of a triangle relate to each other. The name comes from three Greek roots: tri means three, gon means sides, and metron means measure.
keyPoints: Trigonometry begins with right-angled triangles in real life.
It studies the relationship between sides and angles.
Its name means three sides measure.
activities.explanation: Trigonometry helps people find heights and distances using triangles.

activities.title: Turn the angle

tasks.say: Find the angle where sin and cos are equal.
tasks.then: At 45 degrees sin and cos are both about 0.707, and tan is exactly 1.

tasks.say: Make tan bigger than 1.
tasks.then: Past 45 degrees the height beats the width, so tan is more than 1.

tasks.say: Turn the line straight up.
tasks.then: At 90 degrees sin is 1 and cos is 0.

activities.takeaway: sin is the height, cos is the width and tan is the steepness of a line of length 1 at that angle.
activities.explanation: sin is the height, cos is the width and tan is the steepness of a line of length 1 at that angle.

activities.prompt: A balloon is above the ground. How can trigonometry help find its height?
steps: Imagine the balloon directly above a point on the ground.
Its vertical height meets the horizontal ground at a right angle.
Because trigonometry links sides and angles, the triangle can give the altitude.
Therefore, the imagined right triangle helps find the balloon’s height.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A balloon is 3 metres horizontally from the point below it and 4 metres above the ground. What is the length of the balloon's sloping line of sight in metres?
activities.explanation: The right triangle has a horizontal side of 3 metres and a vertical side of 4 metres. The sloping side is found by adding the squares of the two perpendicular sides and taking the square root. The sum of the squares is 25, so the line of sight is 5 metres.
steps: The right triangle has a horizontal side of 3 metres and a vertical side of 4 metres.
The sloping side is found by adding the squares of the two perpendicular sides and taking the square root.
The sum of the squares is 25, so the line of sight is 5 metres.
activities.hint: Use the two perpendicular sides of the right triangle to find the sloping side.

90 - 40 = 50, so the other acute angle is 50 degrees.

activities.title: Meet the Six Trigonometric Ratios
activities.body: In a right triangle, trigonometric ratios are special ratios involving the sides. Angle A is acute. For angle A, BC is opposite, AB is adjacent, and AC is the hypotenuse. The six ratios are sine, cosine, tangent, cosecant, secant, and cotangent. Their short forms include sin A, cos A, and tan A. Cosecant, secant, and cotangent are reciprocal ratios. These ratios connect an angle with its triangle's side lengths.

Cosine is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse, so cos A = 0.6.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: History and Size Independence of Trigonometric Ratios

activities.prompt: Why did “sin” travel from an ancient Indian book to our math classrooms?

activities.title: Sine’s History and Changing Ratios
activities.body: The modern idea of sine was first used in the Aryabhatiyam. Aryabhata’s ardha-jya meant a half-chord, shortened to jya or jiva. Jiva became sinus, meaning curve. Edmund Gunter first used ‘sin’. Cosine arose later to calculate sine of a complementary angle. Sir Jonas Moore first used ‘cos’ in 1674. sin A is not a product. A trigonometric ratio stays unchanged when sides change but the angle stays the same.
keyPoints: Modern sine began with the Aryabhatiyam.
Names changed from ardha-jya to jya or jiva, then sinus and sin.
Ratios stay unchanged when sides change but the angle stays the same.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect the name’s history with the ratio’s size independence.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding Values for 45°, 30° and 60°

activities.prompt: What makes 45°, 30°, and 60° special in a triangle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Angles and Side Ratios
activities.body: A right triangle with a 45° angle has another 45° angle. Its two perpendicular sides are equal. AC is the hypotenuse, used with sine and cosine. BC is opposite the 45° angle. AB is next to it. Sine uses BC and AC. Cosine uses AB and AC. Tangent uses BC and AB. An equilateral triangle has three 60° angles. A perpendicular makes equal halves and equal angles. The smaller right triangle has 30° and 60° angles.
keyPoints: The two perpendicular sides of the 45° triangle are equal.
Sine uses BC and AC; cosine uses AB and AC.
The smaller right triangle has 30° and 60° angles.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Special Angles and Their Uses

activities.prompt: What happens to sine, cosine, and tangent at familiar special angles?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Special-angle values
activities.body: At 0°, sine is 0, cosine is 1, tangent is 0, and secant is 1. Cotangent is not defined at 0°. Tangent is also not defined at 90°. From 0° to 90°, sine increases from 0 to 1. Meanwhile, cosine decreases from 1 to 0.

Tangent is not defined at 90°.
Sine increases while cosine decreases from 0° to 90°.
activities.explanation: You can use these special-angle values as quick checks.

activities.prompt: A ladder is 10 cm long and makes a 90° angle with the floor. Using sine at 90°, what is the length of the ladder's vertical side in cm?
steps: The ladder's length is 10 cm.

The answer is 10 cm.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Trigonometric Identities

activities.prompt: Can one trigonometric ratio reveal an entire right triangle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Key ideas
activities.body: An identity is an equation that is true for every value of its variables. A trigonometric identity involves trigonometric ratios. In right triangle ABC, AB squared plus BC squared equals AC squared. Another identity is sin squared A plus cos squared A equals 1. This identity holds for angles from 0° to 90°. Knowing one trigonometric ratio lets you determine the other ratios.
keyPoints: An identity is true for every value of its variables.
sin squared A plus cos squared A equals 1.
One trigonometric ratio can help determine the others.
activities.explanation: These are the key relationships you will use in this lesson.

activities.prompt: In a right triangle, sin A is 3 out of 5 and cos A is 4 out of 5. What is the sum of sin squared A and cos squared A?
steps: The sine ratio is 3 out of 5, and the cosine ratio is 4 out of 5.
Their squares are 0.36 and 0.64.
The squared sine plus the squared cosine is one, so 0.36 plus 0.64 = 1.

gen.template: In a right triangle, sin A is {s} out of {h} and cos A is {c} out of {h}. What is the sum of sin squared A and cos squared A?
steps: The sine ratio is {s} out of {h}, and the cosine ratio is {c} out of {h}.
Their squares are {sin2} and {cos2}.
The squared sine plus the squared cosine is one, so {sin2} plus {cos2} = {answer}.
gen.hint: Use the identity that the squared sine plus the squared cosine is one.

activities.explanation: Watch how it is solved.

activities.prompt: A roof model forms right triangle ABC. You know sin A. Can you find the other ratios?
steps: Use sin² A + cos² A = 1, since it links the ratios.
Rearrange it to get cos A = √(1 − sin² A).
This works because cosine can use one minus sine squared.
Then use sine and cosine, because one ratio determines the other ratios.
So both missing ratios can be found from the known sine ratio.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Always true
activities.prompt: An identity is true for every value of its variables.
activities.explanation: This is the main meaning of an identity.

activities.prompt: In right triangle ABC, AB is 3 cm and BC is 12 cm. What is AC squared in square cm?
activities.explanation: AB is 3 cm and BC is 12 cm. The right-triangle rule says that the squares of the two legs add to the hypotenuse square. So AC squared is 3 squared plus 12 squared, giving 153 = 153 square cm.
steps: AB is 3 cm and BC is 12 cm.
The right-triangle rule says that the squares of the two legs add to the hypotenuse square.
So AC squared is 3 squared plus 12 squared, giving 153 = 153 square cm.
activities.hint: Use the right-triangle rule on the two legs.

So AC squared is {a} squared plus {b} squared, giving {hyp2} = {answer} square cm.
gen.hint: Use the right-triangle rule on the two legs.

activities.explanation: The sine ratio is 6 out of 15. Squaring it gives 0.16. One minus that value is 0.84 = 0.84.
steps: The sine ratio is 6 out of 15.
Squaring it gives 0.16.
One minus that value is 0.84 = 0.84.
activities.hint: Square the sine ratio, then subtract it from one.

activities.explanation: The identity is true from 0° to 90°, not only at 90°.

activities.prompt: An identity must be true for every value. A student checks sin² A + cos² A once. Is this enough?
options: No. One angle cannot prove an equation true for every value.
Yes. One correct check proves an equation true for every value.
No. The equation works only after checking it twice.
Yes. Every checked angle must equal one for an identity.

why.Yes. One correct check proves an equatio: This confuses checking one case with proving every value.
why.No. The equation works only after checki: Checking twice still does not check every value of the variable.
why.Yes. Every checked angle must equal one: This wrongly says an identity requires an angle to equal one.

activities.explanation: One angle is not every value, so it cannot prove an identity.

activities.prompt: AB² + BC² = AC² in right triangle ABC. You know AB and AC. How can you find BC?
options: Subtract AB² from AC², then take the square root.
Add AB² to AC², then take the square root.
Multiply AB² by AC², then take the square root.
Divide AC² by AB², then take the square root.

why.Add AB² to AC², then take the square roo: The two side squares are added, so adding AB² cannot isolate BC².
why.Multiply AB² by AC², then take the squar: The rule adds side squares, but this wrongly multiplies them.
why.Divide AC² by AB², then take the square: The rule adds side squares, but this wrongly divides them.

activities.explanation: Rearranging the rule gives BC² = AC² − AB².

activities.context: A student stands on a balcony overlooking a river and tries to find its width. The student imagines a right triangle connecting the balcony to the opposite bank. The top of Qutub Minar can be studied in a similar way, and the altitude of a balloon can be found by imagining a right triangle. These methods find heights and distances, so they belong to trigonometry. Early astronomers also used it to find the distances of stars and planets from Earth.
activities.prompt: Based on the balcony situation, what should the student do next to find the river's width?
options: Use the relationship between suitable sides and angles of the imagined right triangle to calculate the width.
Add the lengths of the two perpendicular sides, since both together must equal the river's width.
Use the drawing of the triangle as the measurement, since its shape already shows the width.
Choose the side nearest the student, without considering how its angle relates to the other side.

why.Add the lengths of the two perpendicular: Adding the perpendicular sides would not give the width in general.
why.Use the drawing of the triangle as the m: A drawing is a mathematical model, not a measurement of the river.
why.Choose the side nearest the student, wit: Choosing a side without considering its relationship to an angle is insufficient.

activities.explanation: This applies the side-angle relationship that trigonometry studies.

activities.context: A student stands on a balcony overlooking a river and tries to find its width. The student imagines a right triangle connecting the balcony to the opposite bank. The top of Qutub Minar can be studied in a similar way, and the altitude of a balloon can be found by imagining a right triangle. These methods find heights and distances, so they belong to trigonometry. Early astronomers also used it to find the distances of stars and planets from Earth.
activities.prompt: If an early astronomer wanted to find the distance of a planet from Earth, how should trigonometry be applied?
options: Find the side-angle relationship in a triangle that gives the required distance.
Choose any triangle without relating its sides and angles, since every triangle gives the distance.

activities.body: Trigonometry helps in practical situations. Imagine a student looking at a minar’s top. The line AC joins the student’s eye to that top. It is called the line of sight. The angle between this line and the horizontal is the angle of elevation. Looking above the horizontal means raising your head. Looking down towards a point means lowering your head. That downward angle is the angle of depression.

activities.title: Angles, Buildings, and the River
activities.body: The building example uses two downward angles of depression: 30 and 45 degrees. Line PB crosses parallel lines PQ and BD. Angles QPB and PBD are equal alternate angles. This helps find the tall building’s height and the distance between the buildings. In the river example, a bridge is 3 metres above the banks. Trigonometric ratios can determine heights, lengths, and distances between distant objects.

activities.explanation: Equal alternate angles and trigonometric ratios help find the measurements.

activities.prompt: A bridge is 3 metres above the banks. The angles of depression are 30° and 45°. What is the river's width?
steps: Because the rise is 3 metres, 30° gives AD = 3√3 metres.
Because the rise is 3 metres, 45° gives BD = 3 metres.
AB covers both parts, so its width is AD + BD.
Thus the river is 3(√3 + 1) metres wide.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an angle of elevation and an angle of depression.

This line is called the line of sight, and the angle at the student’s eye is the angle of elevation. activities.title: Lines and circles
activities.body: A circle contains every point at the same distance from one fixed point. This fixed point is the centre. The radius is the constant distance from the centre to the circle's points. Every line through an inside point meets the circle at two points. Through a point on the circle, one and only one tangent passes. Through a point outside, exactly two tangents pass. activities.context: A circular garden has a fixed centre, and every point in the garden is the same distance from that centre. A straight path is checked against the garden. If it shares no point with the garden, there is no meeting. If it meets the garden at one point, it has a single common point. If it meets the garden at two points, it passes through the circle at two places.
activities.prompt: In the case, the straight path shares no point with the circular garden. What should the path be called?
options: A non-intersecting line
A secant
A tangent
A line with two common points

why.A secant: Two common points would make the line a secant.
why.A tangent: One common point would make the line a tangent.
why.A line with two common points: The path has no common point, not two.

activities.explanation: No common point means the line is non-intersecting.

activities.context: A circular garden has a fixed centre, and every point in the garden is the same distance from that centre. A straight path is checked against the garden. If it shares no point with the garden, there is no meeting. If it meets the garden at one point, it has a single common point. If it meets the garden at two points, it passes through the circle at two places.
activities.prompt: If the straight path changes so that it meets the circular garden at exactly one point, what happens?
options: It becomes a tangent to the circle.
It becomes a secant to the circle.
It remains non-intersecting.
It must then have two common points.

A secant requires two common points.
A non-intersecting line has no common point.
Meeting at one point does not give two common points.

activities.explanation: A line meeting a circle at one point is a tangent.

activities.context: A circular garden has a fixed centre, and every point in the garden is the same distance from that centre. A straight path is checked against the garden. If it shares no point with the garden, there is no meeting. If it meets the garden at one point, it has a single common point. If it meets the garden at two points, it passes through the circle at two places.
activities.prompt: If the straight path meets the circular garden at two points, how should its position be described?
options: It is a secant with two common points.
It is a tangent with one common point.
It is non-intersecting with no common point.
It has one common point but is not a tangent.

A tangent has only one common point.
why.It is non-intersecting with no common po: A non-intersecting line has no common point.
why.It has one common point but is not a tan: Meeting at two points does not give one common point.

activities.explanation: Two common points identify the line as a secant.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A straight path that does not meet the circular garden is non-intersecting.
Reason (R): The path has no point in common with the circle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains the statement because having no common point makes the line non-intersecting.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A straight path meeting the circular garden at one point is a tangent.
Reason (R): The path meets the circle at two points.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement is true, but the reason is false because a tangent meets the circle at one point.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a non-intersecting line, a secant, and a tangent.
activities.answer: A non-intersecting line and a circle have no point in common. A secant meets the circle at two points, so it has two common points. A tangent meets the circle at one point, so it has only one common point. These are the three possible positions of a line in relation to a circle. Therefore, the difference depends on the number of common points: none, one, or two. No other position is possible.
points: A non-intersecting line has no common point.
A secant has two common points.
A tangent has one common point.
These are the only three possible positions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A circular wheel moves along a straight line that is tangent to its circular shape. The line touches the wheel at one common point, called the point of contact. As the wheel continues along the line, the contact occurs at another point on the wheel. A student draws the wheel at different positions and wonders whether a second tangent could touch the wheel at the same point of contact.
activities.prompt: At the point of contact shown for one wheel position, what should the student do?
options: Draw one tangent, because only one is possible at that point
Draw two tangents, one in each direction
Draw one secant and call it a tangent
Draw no line because the point is already occupied

why.Draw two tangents, one in each direction: Two tangents at one point would contradict uniqueness.
why.Draw one secant and call it a tangent: A tangent meets the circle at only one point.
why.Draw no line because the point is alread: A tangent exists at every point on the circle.

activities.explanation: Only one tangent exists at a point on a circle.

activities.context: A circular wheel moves along a straight line that is tangent to its circular shape. The line touches the wheel at one common point, called the point of contact. As the wheel continues along the line, the contact occurs at another point on the wheel. A student draws the wheel at different positions and wonders whether a second tangent could touch the wheel at the same point of contact.
activities.prompt: Why does the line remain a tangent as the wheel moves?
options: A tangent is available at every point the wheel reaches.
A tangent must meet the wheel at two points.
The contact point never changes during movement.
Any line beneath a moving wheel is automatically a tangent.

why.A tangent must meet the wheel at two poi: A tangent meets the circle at only one point.
why.The contact point never changes during m: The contact location changes as the wheel moves.
why.Any line beneath a moving wheel is autom: Only a line meeting the circle at one point is a tangent.

activities.explanation: A tangent exists at every point on a circle.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The common point of a tangent and a circle is the point of contact.
Reason (R): The word tangent comes from the Latin word tangere.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the origin of the word does not explain the meaning of the common point.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): More than one tangent can be drawn at the same point of a circle.
Reason (R): There is only one tangent at a point on a circle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because only one tangent exists at each point, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: How does a line change as it moves towards a tangent position?
activities.answer: The chord cut by the line becomes shorter as the line moves towards a tangent position. When the line reaches that position, it meets the circle at only one point. The two ends of the chord of a tangent meet at the same point. This common point is the point of contact, so the tangent touches the circle there. A tangent is therefore a special kind of secant.
points: The chord becomes shorter towards the tangent position.
A tangent meets the circle at only one point.
The chord's two ends meet at the same point.
The common point is the point of contact.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A designer checks a circular component with centre O. At P, a straight edge XY touches the component at exactly one point. The designer draws radius OP and marks point Q on XY away from P. The measurement shows OQ is longer than OP. The designer must explain why OP is the shortest distance from the centre to the edge, why OP is perpendicular to XY, and why no second tangent can touch the component at P.
activities.prompt: The designer moves the marked point Q to another position on XY, still away from P. What must be true about Q?
options: It remains outside the circle.
It lies on the circle.
It lies inside the circle.
It is exactly at P.

A tangent touches the circle only at P.
A point on the tangent away from P cannot be inside the circle.
Q is away from P, and P is the only point of contact.

activities.explanation: Every point on a tangent apart from P lies outside the circle.

activities.context: A designer checks a circular component with centre O. At P, a straight edge XY touches the component at exactly one point. The designer draws radius OP and marks point Q on XY away from P. The measurement shows OQ is longer than OP. The designer must explain why OP is the shortest distance from the centre to the edge, why OP is perpendicular to XY, and why no second tangent can touch the component at P.
activities.prompt: What should the designer conclude if another line through P appears to touch the component at P?
options: That line is not a tangent.
It must be a second tangent.
It must be the normal.
It must touch the circle at another point.

A second tangent at P is therefore not possible.
The normal is the line containing the radius OP, not any line through P.
why.It must touch the circle at another poin: Single-point contact does not mean that a line must touch the circle again elsewhere.

activities.explanation: There can be one and only one tangent at P.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): OP is perpendicular to the tangent XY.
Reason (R): OP is the shortest distance from the centre O to XY.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The shortest distance OP shows that OP is perpendicular to the tangent XY.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point.
Reason (R): There can be one and only one tangent at any point on a circle.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the uniqueness of the tangent does not explain its single point of contact.

activities.prompt: Explain why the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent XY, and identify the name of the line containing OP.
activities.answer: OP is the shortest distance from the centre O to the tangent XY. This shortest distance shows that OP is perpendicular to XY. Since OP is the radius drawn to the point of contact P, the radius to P is at right angles to the tangent. The line containing the radius OP through P is also called the normal. Thus the normal meets the tangent at a right angle, which is the key relationship between a radius to the point of contact and a tangent.
points: OP is the shortest distance from O to XY.
The shortest distance shows that OP is perpendicular to XY.
OP is the radius to the point of contact P.
The line containing OP is called the normal.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

why.One and only one tangent can be drawn fr: One tangent applies to a point on the circle.
why.Two tangent segments of equal lengths ca: Equal tangent lengths apply to an external point.

activities.prompt: Which circle part fits each shape, and what do we call it?

activities.title: Sectors and segments
activities.body: A sector is the circle part enclosed by two radii and their matching arc. A segment is the part between a chord and its matching arc. AB is a chord of the circle with centre O. The angle AOB is the sector’s angle. OAPB is the minor sector, while OAQB is the major sector. APB is the minor segment, while AQB is the major segment.
keyPoints: Two radii and their corresponding arc enclose a sector.
A chord and its corresponding arc enclose a segment.
OAPB is the minor sector.
OAQB is the major sector.
APB is the minor segment.
AQB is the major segment.
activities.explanation: Sectors use two radii, while segments use a chord.

lessons.title: Area of a sector

activities.prompt: How could we find the area of just one slice of a circle?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a sector?
activities.body: A sector is part of a circular region. Its central angle is q, and q is measured in degrees. A whole circular region has angle 360°. Its area is πr². So, a sector with angle q has area q multiplied by πr² and divided by 360. The Unitary Method helps you find this area.
keyPoints: The central angle of a sector is q.
A whole circular region has angle 360°.
Sector area is q multiplied by πr² and divided by 360.
activities.explanation: The sector formula comes from the area of the whole circle.

activities.prompt: A sector has radius 6 cm and central angle 360 degrees. Using π = 3.14, what is its area in cm²?
steps: The radius is 6 cm and the sector angle is 360 degrees.
The whole-circle area is 113.04 cm², and the sector takes 360 out of 360 equal angle parts.
Multiply 113.04 by 360 and divide by 360, giving 113.04 cm².

The whole-circle area is {wholeArea} cm², and the sector takes {q} out of {degrees} equal angle parts.
Multiply {wholeArea} by {q} and divide by {degrees}, giving {answer} cm².
gen.hint: First find the whole-circle area, then take the sector's angle share.

activities.title: Unroll the circle

tasks.say: Double the radius to 8.
tasks.then: The circumference doubled too, but the area became 4 times as big.

tasks.say: Make the smallest circle.
tasks.then: Even a tiny circle is still about 3.14 diameters round.

activities.takeaway: Every circle goes round about 3.14 diameters, which is π. Circumference = 2πr and area = πr².
activities.explanation: Every circle goes round about 3.14 diameters, which is π. Circumference = 2πr and area = πr².

activities.prompt: The area of a 360-degree sector is πr².
activities.explanation: The area of a 360-degree sector equals the area of the whole circle.

activities.prompt: A round coin has radius 3 cm. Using π = 3.14, what is the area of its whole circular face in cm²?
activities.explanation: The radius is 3 cm, and the whole 360-degree region is the circle. Using π as 3.14, the circle's area is 28.26 cm². Therefore, the whole circular area is 28.26 cm².
steps: The radius is 3 cm, and the whole 360-degree region is the circle.
Using π as 3.14, the circle's area is 28.26 cm².

activities.title: Finding a segment area
activities.body: A circle can be split into a minor segment and a major segment. APB is the minor segment, while AQB is the major segment. The segment area equals the sector area minus the triangle area. For segment APB, subtract triangle OAB from sector OAPB. The major segment equals the circle minus the minor segment.
keyPoints: The segment area is the sector area minus the triangle area.
For APB, the corresponding triangle is OAB.
The major segment AQB is the circle minus the minor segment.

activities.title: Finding a major region

The major segment AQB has the circle's area minus the minor-segment area. The major and minor sectors together fill the whole circle. The major and minor segments together also fill the whole circle.

Both pairs of regions share the whole circle's area.

activities.body: These exercises practise circle areas. A sector lies between two radii. A quadrant is one quarter of a circle. A chord links two points on a circle. Exercise 11.1 has radius 6 cm and angle 60°. The brooch uses five diameters to make ten equal sectors. A sector’s area is q × πr² ÷ 360. A segment is its sector’s area minus its triangle’s area.
keyPoints: Exercise 11.1 has radius 6 cm and angle 60°.
A sector’s area is q × πr² ÷ 360.
A segment’s area is its sector’s area minus its triangle’s area.
The brooch uses five diameters and makes ten equal sectors.
activities.explanation: The sector and segment rules connect the exercise details to circle areas.

activities.prompt: A quadrant is one quarter of a circle whose circumference is 20 cm. What is the length of its curved edge in cm?
steps: The full circumference is 20 cm.
A quadrant contains one fourth of the circle, so divide the circumference by 4.
20 divided by 4 = 5 cm.

activities.explanation: The 10 diameters make 20 equal sectors. The angles of all the sectors together make 360°. 360 divided by 20 = 18°.

activities.prompt: At school, a circular badge has radius 20 cm, and a chord subtends a right angle at the centre. Using π = 3.14, what is the area in square cm of the segment between the chord and the arc?
activities.explanation: The badge has radius 20 cm, and the sector angle is 90°. The sector area is 3.14 multiplied by the square of the radius, divided by 4, while the triangle area is the square of the radius divided by 2. 3.14 x 20 x 20 divided by 4 = 314 square cm. 20 x 20 divided by 2 = 200 square cm. 314 - 200 = 114 square cm.
steps: The badge has radius 20 cm, and the sector angle is 90°.
The sector area is 3.14 multiplied by the square of the radius, divided by 4, while the triangle area is the square of the radius divided by 2.
3.14 x 20 x 20 divided by 4 = 314 square cm.
20 x 20 divided by 2 = 200 square cm.
314 - 200 = 114 square cm.
activities.hint: Find the quarter-circle sector area and subtract the right-triangle area.

3.14 x 20 x 20 divided by 10 = 125.6 square cm.
